meta.note: Pieces have a role: answer, situation, did, result, learned, or decoy (hard rounds only). "orders" lists every acceptable order; the first is the model shown in the reveal.

rounds.q: What's one thing you're really good at?

pieces.text: I'm really good at staying organized.
This fall I had soccer three days a week, a part-time job and AP classes.
I kept one calendar on my phone and planned each week on Sunday night.
I didn't miss a single shift or assignment all semester.

rounds.why: Answer first, then prove it: say the strength, then the situation, what you did, and how it turned out.

rounds.q: Tell me about a time something didn't go the way you planned.

pieces.text: Our club's bake sale got rained out, but we still made it work.
We'd planned to sell outside after school, and it poured that afternoon.
I asked the front office if we could use the lobby and made a quick sign to point people inside.
We raised $140, close to our goal.
Now I always plan a backup spot.

rounds.why: Lead with the short version, then tell it in order. Ending with what you learned shows you grew from it.

rounds.q: Tell me about a time you worked with a group.

pieces.text: I helped my chemistry group get organized when we were falling behind.
Two weeks before the project was due, nobody knew who was doing what.
I suggested we split it into four parts and check in at lunch every Wednesday.
We finished a day early and got an A.
Honestly, one guy in our group was really lazy and never did anything.

rounds.decoyWhy: Complaining about a teammate makes you sound hard to work with, even if it's true.
rounds.why: Keep the story about what you did. Blaming others pulls the focus away from you.

rounds.q: Tell me about a mistake you made and what you did next.

pieces.text: I once double-booked myself and almost let my neighbor down.
I'd promised to watch her dog on the same day as an away game.
As soon as I noticed, I called her, apologized and found a friend to cover.
Now everything goes into my phone calendar the moment I agree to it.

rounds.why: Own the mistake up front, show how you fixed it, then what you changed. That order shows responsibility.

rounds.q: What's something you've taught yourself?

pieces.text: I taught myself to edit video.
I wanted to make a highlight reel of my cousin's soccer season.
I watched free tutorials and practiced on short clips every weekend.
Now I make the highlight videos for our school's sports teams.

rounds.why: Say the skill first, then how you learned it and what you can do now. The result is the proof.

rounds.q: What do you do when you feel nervous?

pieces.text: I slow my breathing and remind myself I've prepared.
Before my first piano recital, my hands were shaking.
I'd practiced the first few bars until I could play them without thinking, and I took three slow breaths before I started.
Once I got going, the nerves faded and I played the whole piece.
I also get nervous about a lot of stuff at home, like my parents arguing.

rounds.decoyWhy: Too much personal detail. It's okay to keep private things private in an interview.
rounds.why: Your answer and one example are enough. Stay on what helps you steady yourself.

rounds.q: Tell me about a time you helped someone.

pieces.text: I helped a new student find her place at our school.
She'd moved mid-year and was eating lunch alone every day.
I invited her to our table and showed her where the clubs met.
She joined robotics with me, and now she's one of my closest friends.

rounds.why: Start with what you did in one line, then tell the story. The ending shows why it mattered.

rounds.q: What's something you're working on getting better at?

pieces.text: I'm working on speaking up in class.
I used to stay quiet even when I knew the answer.
This semester I set a goal to say one thing in every history discussion.
Now it feels pretty normal, and my participation grade went up.

rounds.why: Name the weakness, show where you started, then what you're doing about it. Ending on progress keeps it positive.

rounds.q: Tell me about a time you had to keep going after you wanted to quit.

pieces.text: I almost quit cross-country my first season, but I'm glad I didn't.
I finished last in my first three races.
My coach helped me focus on beating my own time instead of other runners.
By the end of the season I'd cut two minutes off.
I learned that small goals keep me going when big ones feel impossible.
Cross-country is way harder than people think, and the uniforms are ugly.

rounds.decoyWhy: Off-topic. Complaining about the sport doesn't help your story.
rounds.why: Answer first, then the struggle, what changed, the result and the lesson. Extra comments just get in the way.

rounds.q: Tell me about a time you disagreed with someone.

pieces.text: My lab partner and I disagreed about how to run an experiment, and we settled it by testing both ways.
He wanted to skip a step to finish faster, and I was worried our results would be off.
I explained why, and suggested we try both methods on a small sample.
Mine gave cleaner results, and he was fine with it because we'd checked.

rounds.why: The answer up front tells them it ended well. Then the details show how calmly you handled it.

rounds.q: What's a responsibility you have at home?

pieces.text: I take care of my two younger sisters after school.
I pick them up, make them a snack and get them started on homework until my mom gets home at six.
It's taught me to be on time, because they're counting on me.

rounds.why: Not every answer needs a long story. Say it, show what it involves, and what it taught you.

rounds.q: Why should we pick you?

pieces.text: You need someone dependable who's good with people, and that's me.
For the past year I've worked the front desk at my mom's salon on Saturdays.
I greet people, answer the phone and keep the appointment book straight, even when it's packed.
My mom says the regulars ask for me by name now.
Also, I really need the money for a new phone.

rounds.decoyWhy: It's about what you get, not what you'd give them.
rounds.why: Answer what they need, then prove you can do it. Keep the focus on what you offer.

rounds.q: How do you handle having a lot to do at once?

pieces.text: I write everything down and do whatever's due soonest first.
During finals week I also had soccer and two babysitting jobs.
Each night I planned the next day, down to when I'd study.
I got through all of it without missing anything or panicking.

rounds.why: Say your method first. The busy week is the proof that it actually works.

rounds.q: Tell me about something you're proud of.

pieces.text: I'm proud of the lunch club I started at my school.
I noticed a lot of people sat alone or stared at their phones during lunch.
I started a club where people teach each other a skill, like chess or knitting.
It grew to about 30 people.
It showed me I can start something from nothing if I just ask people to join.

rounds.why: Name it, then tell why you started it and what happened. The result and the lesson can go in either order.

rounds.q: Tell me about a time you got feedback you didn't like.

pieces.text: My English teacher told me my essays were too wordy, and she was right.
I'd gotten a C on an essay I thought was great, and it stung.
I asked her to show me two examples, then started cutting every sentence that didn't add something.
My next two essays got A's.
My old English teacher never gave anyone good grades anyway.

rounds.decoyWhy: Blaming a teacher undercuts the whole point, which is that you can take feedback.
rounds.why: Admitting the feedback was fair, then showing what you changed, is the strongest version.

rounds.q: Tell me about a time you took the lead.

pieces.text: I took the lead on our family's yard sale this spring.
We had a garage full of stuff and no plan, and my parents were busy.
I sorted everything, priced it, made signs and got my brothers to run the tables.
We made over $600 and cleared out the garage.

rounds.why: Leading can happen anywhere, even at home. Answer first, then show the steps you took.

rounds.q: Tell me about a time you had to learn something quickly.

pieces.text: I had to learn to run the scoreboard in one afternoon.
The usual volunteer got sick right before a home basketball game.
I asked the athletic director for a ten-minute walkthrough, wrote down the buttons and practiced during warm-ups.
The game ran without a single mistake on the board.
Asking for a quick demo is faster than guessing.

rounds.why: Start with what you learned to do, then how. Your lesson can come before or after the result.

rounds.q: How would your friends describe you?

pieces.text: They'd say I'm the one who shows up.
If someone needs a ride to practice or help moving, I'm usually the one they text.
My friend Maya calls me the group's backup plan.
Some people at school think I'm kind of annoying, but whatever.

rounds.decoyWhy: Adds a negative nobody asked about.
rounds.why: One quality, backed by what you do and what a friend says. That's the whole answer.

rounds.q: Tell me about a time you were reliable when it counted.

pieces.text: I walk my neighbor's dog every weekday, and I've never missed a day.
Last winter a snowstorm closed school and most roads.
I still walked over at noon, because I knew the dog had no one else.
She's kept me on for two years and recommended me to two other neighbors.

rounds.why: Lead with the claim, then the moment that proves it. The result shows others trust you.

rounds.q: What would you do if a customer was upset with you?

pieces.text: I'd stay calm, listen, and try to fix it, or get a manager if I couldn't.
At our school book fair, a parent got upset about a price.
I apologized, listened to what she expected, and got the teacher in charge.
It turned out to be a wrong sticker, and she left happy.

rounds.why: Say your plan first, then show you've done it before. That makes your plan believable.

rounds.q: Have you ever handled money?

pieces.text: Not at a register yet, but I ran the cash box at our team's car wash.
I counted the money at the start and end of each of the three Saturdays.
It matched every time.
I'm careful with change, and I'd be glad to learn your system.
At my last babysitting job the parents paid me late, which was really annoying.

rounds.decoyWhy: A complaint about someone you worked for. It makes employers wonder what you'd say about them.
rounds.why: Be honest about no register experience, then point to the closest thing you've done.

rounds.q: Why do you want to work here?

pieces.text: I want to be part of a team like yours.
My family comes here a lot, and the staff always stay friendly even when it's packed.
I want to learn how to handle a busy rush like that.

rounds.why: Say why, then show you know the place, then what you hope to learn.

rounds.q: Tell me about a time you went above what was asked.

pieces.text: At my aunt's bakery, I started folding cake boxes without being asked.
I'd finished my tasks early one Saturday and everyone else was busy.
I watched how they folded the boxes and made a stack for the afternoon orders.
It saved the team about half an hour during the rush, and now it's my job every week.

rounds.why: The result shows the extra effort made a difference, which is what makes the story land.

rounds.q: How would you handle a really busy shift?

pieces.text: I'd stay calm and take things one at a time.
Last summer I helped at the pool's snack stand on the Fourth of July.
The line was huge, so I took orders while my coworker made them, and we switched when one of us fell behind.
We sold out of almost everything and never had a mix-up.
To be honest, I hate crowds and loud places.

rounds.decoyWhy: Off-message. It argues against you for this job.
rounds.why: Answer first, then a real busy day. Teamwork in the story shows how you'd fit in.

rounds.q: Why are you interested in this school?

pieces.text: Mostly because of your hands-on environmental science program.
First-years here can do field research at the nature preserve, which almost no other school offers.
At the info session I talked to a student who said classes are small and professors know your name.
That matters to me because I learn best by asking a lot of questions.

rounds.why: Say your main reason, give the details that only fit this school, then tie it to you.

rounds.q: Tell me about a class that challenged you.

pieces.text: Pre-calc challenged me more than any class so far.
I got a 61 on the first test, which honestly scared me.
I started going to my teacher's help sessions on Tuesdays and redoing every problem I got wrong.
I finished the year with a B+.
I'm not afraid of hard classes anymore, because I know what to do.

rounds.why: Name the class, then the struggle, the fix and the result. The lesson shows you'd handle college work.

rounds.q: What do you want to study?

pieces.text: I'm undecided, but I keep coming back to psychology and education.
I volunteer at an after-school program twice a week.
I've noticed some kids light up with one tutor and shut down with another, and I want to understand why.
So I'd like to take classes in both during my first year and see which fits.
My parents want me to be a doctor, but I don't really care what they think.

rounds.decoyWhy: Family drama that doesn't help your answer.
rounds.why: Being undecided is fine. Show what you're drawn to and why, then your plan to explore it.

rounds.q: How would you contribute to our campus?

pieces.text: I'd bring the kind of club I started in high school.
At my school I started a lunch club where people teach each other a skill.
It grew to about 30 people from all different friend groups.
I'd love to start something like it here, or join a club that does something similar.

rounds.why: What you've already done is the best preview of what you'd add. End by connecting it to their campus.

rounds.q: What do you do outside of school?

pieces.text: I work at my family's restaurant on weekends.
Lately I've been helping my dad with the books and ordering supplies.
It's gotten me interested in business, which I'd like to study.

rounds.why: Short and clear: what you do, a detail, and why it matters for what's next.

rounds.q: Is there anything else you'd like us to know?

pieces.text: Yes. My grades dipped in tenth grade, and I'd like to explain why.
My grandma moved in with us that year, and I helped care for her after school.
I learned to plan my homework around her schedule and to ask teachers for help early.
My grades have gone up every semester since.
Also, my old counselor didn't help me at all with my applications.

rounds.decoyWhy: A complaint that pulls focus from your growth.
rounds.why: Context plus growth is a strong way to use this question. Leave out complaints.
